questions.q: What IS this feature in one sentence?
questions.a: Controls the visual appearance (ground color, fog, atmosphere tint, lighting temperature) per biome zone so each biome feels visually distinct.

questions.q: What wider system does it belong to?
questions.a: The planet_surface rung — biome visual identity is part of surface-level procedural generation.

questions.q: What would break if this feature didn't exist?
questions.a: All biomes would look identical — the player would navigate by UI markers instead of visual recognition of terrain type.

questions.q: What existing feature does this most resemble?
questions.a: planet_surface (the parent rung) — both define how the world looks at a macro scale.

questions.q: Is this a rung, a sub-rung, or a parameter?
questions.a: Sub-rung of planet_surface, sitting alongside ground_terrain and solar_system in the composition ladder.

questions.q: What physical constraint does it encode?
questions.a: Latitude-temperature mapping: polar biomes have blue-white lighting (6500K), equatorial biomes have warm orange (3500K). Ground color shifts from tan/brown (desert) to white/gray (arctic).

questions.q: What is the ONE measurement that proves it works?
questions.a: A pixel sample from the center of any biome zone predicts the biome type with >90% accuracy based on RGB + temperature-color values.

questions.q: What wall must it never violate?
questions.a: Must never produce visual discomfort: no strobing transitions (blend over >2s), no pure-black zones in walkable areas, no 100% saturation colors.

questions.q: What would a degenerate winner look like?
questions.a: All biomes set to the same grey fog with saturation=0 — technically distinct by parameter but visually identical.

questions.q: How would we know if the constraint is too loose?
questions.a: If two adjacent biomes (e.g., desert and scrubland) have indistinguishable fog color and ground tint, the visual constraint is too loose.

questions.q: What scale does this feature operate at?
questions.a: Per-biome-region, evaluated when the player crosses a biome boundary (~1 transition per 30-120 seconds of walking).

questions.q: What is the right definition level for this scale?
questions.a: Parameter-level: 6 variables per biome (ground_color_rgb, fog_color_rgb, fog_density, atmosphere_tint_kelvin, light_angle_offset, postprocess_contrast).

questions.q: Could this be decomposed further? Into what?
questions.a: Could split into per-channel color parameters, but one RGB triplet per biome is sufficient for the visible range.

questions.q: At what resolution does the pattern emerge?
questions.a: Pattern emerges when the player walks from one biome to another and sees the fog/ground/light colors shift within 3 seconds of crossing the boundary.

questions.q: What would 'deep enough' look like for this feature?
questions.a: When a player can identify their biome type from a screenshot with 90% accuracy without UI aids.

questions.q: What element catalog variables does this train?
questions.a: ground_color_map, fog_color_map, atmosphere_tint_map, biome_light_temperature.

questions.q: How many relevant elements exist in the catalog?
questions.a: 112 catalog entries tagged 'biome' and 'visual' — extensive material and postprocess data.

questions.q: Are there enough variables to train meaningfully?
questions.a: Yes — 6 parameters per biome with 112 catalog references for material parameter grounding.

questions.q: What variables are MISSING from the catalog?
questions.a: Seasonal visual variation (the planet has no orbit axis tilt modeled in the current generation).

questions.q: Would training this require GPU acceleration?
questions.a: No — parameter count (6 * 8 biomes = 48) is well below the 1000-variable GPU threshold.

questions.q: Does this feature connect to the Mirror of Erised?
questions.a: Indirectly — visual differentiation makes biome-specific resource knowledge a learnable skill. A red-tinted sky tells the player 'this biome has iron.'

questions.q: How directly does it serve the Mirror? (direct/enabling/orthogonal)
questions.a: Enabling — visual cues teach the player which resources are available, enabling strategic giving.

questions.q: Would a costless life still be meaningful without this feature?
questions.a: Yes — the Mirror works without visual variety. But the world would feel like a grey box, diminishing the emotional weight of giving.

questions.q: Could this feature be gamed to fake a generous life?
questions.a: No — visual appearance is passive. The player cannot manipulate color values to fake biome knowledge.

questions.q: What would this feature look like if it perfectly served the Mirror?
questions.a: Every biome has an iconic color palette the player learns to read: 'Orange sky = desert = sand to give. Green sky = forest = wood to give.'

questions.q: What other features does this compose with?
questions.a: planet_surface (parent), ground_terrain (texture blending), solar_system (skybox tint), biome_resources (resource color cues).

questions.q: What could break at the seam between this and its neighbors?
questions.a: ground_terrain material color overrides the biome ground color — terrain texture and biome fog could clash visually.

questions.q: Does this need a decoder step to place in the level?
questions.a: Yes — the decoder must set post-process volumes and ExponentialHeightFog per biome region.

questions.q: What would a failed composition look like?
questions.a: ground_terrain has lush green textures but biome_visuals has red desert fog — visual dissonance breaks immersion.

questions.q: Does this feature need a human judgment or can the system verify it?
questions.a: System verifies RGB-distance between adjacent biomes (minimum delta-E threshold). Human judges whether the visual difference feels natural.

questions.q: How many generations to converge?
questions.a: ~80 generations at pop=64 for 48-parameter multi-biome color space.

questions.q: What population size is appropriate?
questions.a: 64 — need enough diversity to explore color combinations across 8 biomes simultaneously.

questions.q: What's the risk of overfitting?
questions.a: Medium — a winner could memorize specific RGB values for one terrain seed and produce garish colors on another seed.

questions.q: What's the risk of underfitting?
questions.a: Medium — if delta-E constraint between adjacent biomes is too weak, two biomes may look identical.

questions.q: Does the existing trainer support this domain type?
questions.a: Yes — core.trainer handles color-parameter optimization with RGB distance evaluation functions.

questions.q: Have we gone deep enough on this feature?
questions.a: Yes — 48 parameters across 8 biomes with a visual-distinctness wall is adequate for a mid-level sub-rung.

questions.q: What would the NEXT level of decomposition look like?
questions.a: Per-biome material graph: one dedicated master material instance per biome type with unique noise blending patterns.

questions.q: If we stopped here, the game feel complete?
questions.a: Partially — biomes would be visually distinct but materials would use shared shader networks. Good enough for production.

questions.q: What is the human's expected emotional response to this feature?
questions.a: Spatial orientation — 'I know where I am by how it looks.' The visual identity of each biome anchors the player in the world.

questions.q: Does this feature exist because the Mirror demands it, or because it's technically interesting?
questions.a: Technically interesting — visual variety is game-feel polish, not Mirror-critical. But it enables the player to read the world, which serves the Mirror indirectly.
